


                                    DOSSIER BINARY FORMAT 1.0
                                         Elias A. Murphy

                                        Rev. 1, 09.22.2026



1. ABSTRACT
===========

Dossier is a binary format for ASCII documents presented in a 98-column text layout. It stores
metadata and document content in independently compressed sections, allowing a reader to inspect
the document's identity and revision information before decoding its content. Typed content
records describe the document structure and preserve the layout of ASCII diagrams.

This specification defines Dossier version 1.0, including its binary encoding, validation
requirements, and canonical text presentation. Embedded attachments and revision history are
outside its scope, as are encryption and digital signatures.


2. CONVENTIONS AND TERMINOLOGY
==============================

The requirement terms MUST, MUST NOT, and MAY, when written in uppercase, carry the meanings
defined by BCP 14 in RFC 2119[1] and RFC 8174[2].

An octet is an eight-bit byte. Lengths are measured in bytes unless another unit is given, and
file offsets start at zero. Numbers are decimal unless identified as hexadecimal. In a hexadecimal
byte sequence, each pair of digits represents one byte; spaces separate the pairs for readability.

The terms writer and reader refer to implementations that encode and decode Dossier files. A
renderer produces the canonical text representation specified in Section 7. Conformance covers the
document's structure and presentation as well as its binary encoding.

Version information has two levels: the header identifies the container layout, and the
dsx_version metadata field identifies the document schema. The revision field belongs to the
document itself and records its revision number.


3. FILE STRUCTURE
=================

A Dossier file, conventionally named with a .dsx extension, consists of three contiguous parts: a
32-byte header, a compressed metadata section, and a compressed content section. The header gives
the stored lengths M and C, which determine the section boundaries and total file size shown
below.

Offset 0                       Offset 32                  Offset 32 + M
+------------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+
| Header: 32 bytes             | Metadata: M bytes        | Content: C bytes         |
+------------------------------+--------------------------+--------------------------+
                                                         File size: 32 + M + C

The file signature identifies the format. A reader MUST verify it before interpreting the header.
The content section ends at the end of the file.

3.1 HEADER

The header occupies the first 32 bytes without padding. Its fixed-width integer fields are
unsigned and little-endian; the signature is stored as the eight literal bytes listed in the
table.

+--------+-------+------------------------------------------+
| Offset | Bytes | Field                                    |
+--------+-------+------------------------------------------+
| 0      | 8     | Signature: 89 44 53 58 0D 0A 1A 0A (hex) |
| 8      | 1     | Container layout version: 1              |
| 9      | 1     | Compression identifier: 1                |
| 10     | 2     | Reserved: 0                              |
| 12     | 4     | Compressed metadata length, M            |
| 16     | 4     | Uncompressed metadata length             |
| 20     | 4     | Compressed content length, C             |
| 24     | 4     | Uncompressed content length              |
| 28     | 4     | CRC-32 of bytes 0 through 27             |
+--------+-------+------------------------------------------+

The final field contains the CRC-32/ISO-HDLC checksum of the preceding 28 bytes, stored as a
little-endian 32-bit value. The ASCII sequence 123456789 has the check value CBF43926 in
hexadecimal.

For this version, both the container layout version and compression identifier are 1, and the
reserved field is zero. Readers MUST reject headers with other values or an incorrect checksum.

3.2 COMPRESSION

Each section is encoded as an independent zlib stream under RFC 1950[3], using DEFLATE under RFC
1951[4] with no preset dictionary. The zlib framing and Adler-32 checksum follow RFC 1950's
byte-order rules. Readers MUST accept any valid compression level.

A stored section contains one complete stream ending at the declared section boundary. Its decoded
length MUST equal the uncompressed length in the header. The metadata has a nonempty decoded
representation; the content may decode to zero bytes while retaining its complete zlib framing.

3.3 SECTION LENGTHS

Stored section lengths include the zlib framing and checksum. The limits below apply to the values
declared in the header and to the actual section sizes.

+----------+----------------------+----------------------------+
| Section  | Maximum stored bytes | Maximum uncompressed bytes |
+----------+----------------------+----------------------------+
| Metadata | 131072               | 65536                      |
| Content  | 68157440             | 67108864                   |
+----------+----------------------+----------------------------+

M, C, and the uncompressed metadata length are positive. A reader MUST verify that the file
contains exactly 32 + M + C bytes and validate the header before allocating buffers from its
length fields. Decompression MUST remain within the declared uncompressed lengths and the section
limits.


4. PRIMITIVE ENCODING
=====================

4.1 UNSIGNED INTEGERS

U denotes an integer from 0 through 4294967295 encoded in canonical unsigned LEB128. Each byte
carries seven value bits, starting with the least significant group; bit 7 indicates that another
byte follows. The canonical representation uses the shortest encoding and occupies at most five
bytes.

For example, the hexadecimal encodings of 127 and 128 are 7F and 80 01. The sequence 80 00 is
invalid because zero has the one-byte encoding 00. Readers MUST reject noncanonical or truncated
encodings and values outside the permitted range.

4.2 STRINGS

S denotes U(byte_length) followed by that many printable ASCII bytes, with no terminator.
Printable ASCII spans hexadecimal 20 through 7E. S may be empty unless its field requires a
nonempty value.

ASCII(text) denotes the same character encoding with its length supplied by the enclosing field or
record. ASCII blocks extend this repertoire with LF, hexadecimal 0A, to preserve line boundaries.
Other control characters, including tabs, CR, and DEL, are excluded from stored text.

4.3 FIELDS AND RECORDS

Metadata and content use type-length-value encoding, abbreviated TLV. A one-byte type identifier
is followed by U(length) and exactly length value bytes. Inline records use the same layout.

+-------------------+----------------------+--------------------------------+
| Type: one byte    | Value byte length: U | Value: exactly that many bytes |
+-------------------+----------------------+--------------------------------+

Type identifiers are interpreted in the context of their enclosing metadata section, content
section, or inline sequence. Parsing continues through complete TLVs until that enclosing value is
exhausted. Incomplete records and residual bytes are invalid.


5. METADATA
===========

5.1 REQUIRED FIELDS

The metadata section begins with the following five fields, each occurring exactly once in the
order shown. The TLV value length supplies the length of ordinary text fields; S prefixes are used
for names within the authors list.

+----+-------------+---------------------------------------+
| ID | Name        | Value encoding                        |
+----+-------------+---------------------------------------+
| 1  | dsx_version | ASCII(1.0)                            |
| 2  | title       | ASCII(title)                          |
| 3  | authors     | U(count), followed by count S strings |
| 4  | revision    | ASCII(decimal revision number)        |
| 5  | date        | ASCII(MM.DD.YYYY)                     |
+----+-------------+---------------------------------------+

The dsx_version field contains the ASCII value 1.0. Its complete uncompressed TLV is 01 03 31 2E
30 in hexadecimal. This value selects the schema defined by the following field and record
requirements.

The title consists of 1 through 98 printable ASCII characters with no leading or trailing spaces.
It contains at least one uppercase letter and no lowercase letters.

Authors are stored as an ordered list of one or more names. Each name has 1 through 98 printable
ASCII characters, with no leading or trailing spaces and no capitalization restriction. The list
order is preserved through encoding and presentation.

The revision is stored as the ASCII digits of a positive decimal integer, without a sign or
leading zeros, and is limited to 4294967295. The date uses ten ASCII characters in the form
MM.DD.YYYY and identifies a valid Gregorian date in years 0001 through 9999.

5.2 ADDITIONAL FIELDS

Additional metadata follows the required fields in ascending ASCII key order. Each entry uses type
128 with a value composed of S(key) and the remaining bytes as printable ASCII text. The text
value may be empty.

Keys are unique within the section, match [a-z][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}, and differ from the names of the
required fields. Values are flat text strings. A reader MAY retain an unfamiliar key without
interpreting its value; applications rewriting a document MUST preserve these fields except where
the requested edit changes or removes them.


6. DOCUMENT CONTENT
===================

6.1 RECORD TYPES

The content section is a sequence of records in document order. Its uncompressed length delimits
the sequence, which has no separate count or terminator. The record types are listed below.

+----+-------------+-------------------------+
| ID | Record      | Value encoding          |
+----+-------------+-------------------------+
| 1  | Heading     | U(depth) + ASCII(title) |
| 2  | Paragraph   | Sequence of inline TLVs |
| 3  | Bullet item | Sequence of inline TLVs |
| 4  | ASCII block | Printable ASCII and LF  |
| 5  | Reference   | U(number) + ASCII(URL)  |
+----+-------------+-------------------------+

Reference records form the final group and are ordered by strictly increasing number.

6.2 HEADINGS

Heading depth ranges from 1 through 8. The first heading has depth 1; a later heading may have the
same or a smaller depth, or be one level deeper. Section numbering follows record order: each
heading increments the counter at its depth and resets the counters below it.

A heading title is nonempty printable ASCII with at least one uppercase letter, no lowercase
letters, and no leading or trailing spaces. The complete heading, including its generated section
number and separating space, fits within 98 columns.

6.3 PARAGRAPHS AND BULLET ITEMS

Paragraphs and bullet items consist of inline TLVs. Type 1 stores nonempty printable ASCII text;
type 2 stores exactly one U citation number in the range 1 through 4294967295. Writers MUST merge
adjacent text records, while readers interpret such records as consecutive text.

Display text is formed by concatenating text records and rendering each citation as [n]. The
complete paragraph or bullet item is nonempty, with single internal spaces and no leading or
trailing spaces. These whitespace rules apply across record boundaries, allowing a space at either
end of an individual text record. Wrapping and indentation are supplied by the renderer.

Record types carry the citation semantics: a type-1 record containing [1] remains literal text,
while a type-2 record with value 1 refers to reference 1. Both render as [1].

The paragraph Hi illustrates the nested encoding. Its uncompressed bytes are 02 04 01 02 48 69 in
hexadecimal: a type-2 content record whose four-byte value is a type-1 inline record containing
the two ASCII characters.

6.4 ASCII BLOCKS

An ASCII block holds printable ASCII and LF with its layout preserved byte for byte, including
blank lines and trailing spaces. The value may be empty. Each line is at most 98 characters long.

6.5 REFERENCES

Each reference pairs a unique number from 1 through 4294967295 with an absolute URL. The URL is
printable ASCII without spaces and begins with a scheme matching [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*:. Reading
and rendering operate on this stored text without fetching the referenced resource.

Every citation resolves to one reference. The reference group may also include uncited entries.
Section 7.4 defines their presentation and the width limit for the reference URL.


7. CANONICAL PRESENTATION
=========================

7.1 GENERAL RULES

The canonical representation is monospaced text, limited to 98 characters per line, with LF line
endings and a final LF. The renderer supplies layout whitespace around the stored content and
wraps prose at spaces, taking as many whole words as fit on each line. Hyphenated words remain
whole.

The available width includes generated prefixes such as bullet indentation. An unbreakable token
exceeding that width makes the document invalid. ASCII blocks retain their stored layout.

7.2 TITLE BLOCK

The document opens with three empty lines, followed by the title and one line per author in
metadata order. After one empty line comes Rev. N, MM.DD.YYYY. Three more empty lines complete the
block and separate it from any content that follows.

Each nonempty line is centered by adding floor((98 - line_length) / 2) leading spaces, with no
trailing padding. This places the extra column on the right when equal padding on both sides is
impossible.

7.3 SECTION HEADINGS

Depth-1 headings use the form 1. TITLE and are followed immediately by an equals-sign separator
matching the complete heading's character count. Deeper headings use dotted numbers, such as 1.1
TITLE and 1.1.1 TITLE, without a separator.

Between content records, the following record determines the gap: two empty lines before a depth-1
heading, none between consecutive references, and one for all other transitions. The first content
record follows the three empty lines of the title block.

7.4 BODY LAYOUT

A bullet begins with an asterisk and one space. Its continuation lines begin with two spaces,
leaving 96 columns for text on each line. The inter-record spacing in Section 7.3 places one empty
line between adjacent bullet items or paragraphs.

Reference entries MUST use the plaintext form [n] URL, with one space between the citation number
and bare URL. The URL is an unbreakable token subject to the 98-column limit; entries wrap between
[n] and the URL when necessary. Inline citations remain [n].

ASCII blocks retain their exact stored lines within the surrounding layout. Any blank lines at the
beginning or end of a block are additional to the inter-record gap. Their text is neither reflowed
nor trimmed.


8. VALIDATION AND INTEROPERABILITY
==================================

8.1 COMPLETE DOCUMENT VALIDATION

A reader MUST validate the header and declared lengths before decompressing the sections.
Successful decompression requires complete streams with correct checksums and matching expanded
lengths. The resulting metadata and content are then checked against the field definitions and
document rules in Sections 4 through 7.

Readers MUST reject unknown identifiers or unsupported versions. For Dossier 1.0, valid metadata
types are 1 through 5 and 128, content types are 1 through 5, and inline types are 1 and 2. The
dsx_version value is 1.0. Full validation includes metadata ordering, heading transitions,
reference resolution and ordering, and the canonical layout limits.

8.2 METADATA-ONLY INSPECTION

A reader MAY stop after validating the header and total file size, then decompressing and
validating the metadata section. This operation leaves the content section unread and unverified,
which the reader MUST state when reporting its result.

8.3 ENCODING STABILITY

Writers MUST encode the same structured document into the same uncompressed sections. The
prescribed field order and inline-text merging rules establish this representation. Compression
libraries may encode those sections differently while producing conforming files.

8.4 TEXT INTERCHANGE

Text import builds a binary document from an authoring source; export produces the canonical
display. Import is explicit, including for plaintext files previously given a .dsx extension.

Exported text omits additional metadata and gives some distinct record types the same visible
form. Applications MUST therefore treat text exports as lossy presentation copies.


9. SECURITY CONSIDERATIONS
==========================

The length checks in Section 3 bound the memory needed for section data. Readers MUST enforce
these bounds before allocating from declared lengths and throughout decompression. Checksum
failures and incomplete streams fail validation.
